body.heading: The streak that feels impossible
paragraphs: Flip a coin five times and get heads, heads, heads, heads, heads. It feels like a glitch — surely the coin is bent, or luck is running hot, or tails is now 'due'. In fact, the chance of five heads in a specified run of five flips is 1 in 32: uncommon, but nothing like impossible.

Here is the reframe that dissolves the mystery. The sequence HHHHH is exactly as likely as HTHTH, or HHTTH, or any other specific order you care to name — each one also has a chance of 1 in 32. We only gasp at the tidy ones. The coin dealt an ordinary hand; we are the ones who framed it.

body.heading: Every sequence is equally unlikely
paragraphs: Each flip is independent: the coin has no memory of the last result and no plan for the next. After five heads, the chance the next flip is tails is still one half — not higher, because the coin is not keeping score or restoring balance.

Believing tails becomes more likely after a run of heads is called the gambler's fallacy, and it has emptied a great many pockets. Its mirror image — believing a winning streak will continue because someone is 'hot' — is the same error wearing a smile.

body.heading: Try it yourself
paragraphs: Flip a coin twenty times and write down the results honestly, in order. Then look for streaks. You will almost certainly find runs of three or four identical results hiding in there — because in twenty flips, streaks are not surprises. They are what randomness actually looks like.
That is the deeper lesson: real randomness is clumpy. Perfectly alternating, evenly spread results would be the truly suspicious pattern.

takeaway: The coin has no memory: five heads is exactly as likely as any other exact sequence — it just looks more meaningful.
